speechtext: May I ask the Prime Minister whether the press correctly reported a most unusual occasion today, at which the Prime Minister advised the press as to what had taken place in cabinet. In particular, did he say that he had outlined in cabinet in very considerable detail the policy of the government by quoting from statements made by him as well as by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, so it would be clear to every member of the cabinet exactly what the policy was? Did he say "We all agreed that this was the right policy to follow-"

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-ALLEGED DISCLOSURE OF PROCEEDINGS IN CABINET MEETING
speechtext: Order, please. The right hon. gentleman knows that a question has to be asked directly and that it cannot be in the form of requesting confirmation or denial of press reports.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-ALLEGED DISCLOSURE OF PROCEEDINGS IN CABINET MEETING
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege, then. The Prime Minister is reporting what took place in cabinet, and this is so
contrary to constitutional practice that I have to quote what was reported in the press.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-ALLEGED DISCLOSURE OF PROCEEDINGS IN CABINET MEETING
speechtext: I must rule on the question of privilege that there are no exceptions provided in the precedents which would allow the right hon. Leader of the Opposition to put the question in the way he did.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-ALLEGED DISCLOSURE OF PROCEEDINGS IN CABINET MEETING
speechtext: This has never happened before, so there are no precedents. May I ask the Prime Minister this. Did the cabinet agree that the members of the government would follow the policy enunciated in cabinet this morning and say or do nothing which would make its implementation more difficult? I ask the Prime Minister upon what basis the statement was made, and whether there is a precedent for revealing what takes place in cabinet.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: VIET NAM-ALLEGED DISCLOSURE OF PROCEEDINGS IN CABINET MEETING
speechtext: Oh, Mr. Speaker, there are lots of precedents for telling the press the subject matters discussed in cabinet. My right hon. friend will recall many occasions when he indicated what was discussed or not discussed in cabinet. There is no precedent for giving the details of cabinet discussions on any matter, nor was that done this morning. I merely said, and it was quite in order to say so, that the cabinet reaffirmed its adherence to the policy adopted by the government in regard to Viet Nam, in view of the questions that had been raised about that policy in the house and elsewhere. All members of the cabinet not only reaffirmed their confidence in the wisdom of that policy but they all reaffirmed that they would say nothing or do nothing to make more difficult its implementation. I am sure my right hon. friend will be the first to congratulate us on this reaffirmation of cabinet solidarity.

subsubtopic: VIET NAM-ALLEGED DISCLOSURE OF PROCEEDINGS IN CABINET MEETING

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to address a question to the Minister of Agriculture. subtopic: ALBERTA-ASSISTANCE TO FARMERS FOLLOWING STORM DAMAGE

subtopic: ALBERTA-ASSISTANCE TO FARMERS FOLLOWING STORM DAMAGE
speechtext: A further supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Has the Minister of Agriculture initiated any discussion of this matter with the provincial premier?

subtopic: ALBERTA-ASSISTANCE TO FARMERS FOLLOWING STORM DAMAGE

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, at the close of the debate last night I had made some remarks indicating that I felt the system of criminal justice in this country was heavily weighted against the individual, and particularly in connection with the provision for custody pending trial and bail. I also indicated that I should like to discuss this under a second heading, the question of availability of counsel before trial. As will be clear to hon. members from Professor Friedland's remarks which I read last night, the problem of custody before trial is directly related to the question of counsel before trial.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Order, please. May we please have more order. I am sure it is difficult for the members in the chamber to follow the hon. member's remarks.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The question recently has been before the highest court in our country, the Supreme Court of Canada, in the case of Regina v. O'Connor. In that case, a motorist had been taken into custody on suspicion of impaired driving and was submitted to a number of tests by the police at the police station without being informed that he was under arrest, and that he had a right to refuse to submit to the tests, without having the opportunity to seek independent legal advice. Only after being tested was he advised that he was under arrest and only at that time was he given permission to seek legal assistance. He was permitted to make one telephone call. When his solicitor happened not to be there, he was denied a further right to seek assistance.
The Canadian Bill of Rights appears to be quite clear in this regard. It affirms the right of the individual to equality before the law and the protection of the law. It goes on to prohibit any law of Canada from being construed or applied so as to-
-deprive a person who has been arrested or detained
(i)	of the right to be informed promptly of the reason for his arrest or detention, and
(ii)	of the right to retain and instruct counsel without delay...
Prima facie it would appear that the Bill of Rights applies directly to the situation. The Supreme Court of Canada, however, has held that those provisions did not assist the accused under those circumstances. In my opinion the Supreme Court's judgment, which 1 do not deny was probably correct on the law as it stands, has indicated a very fundamental gap in our system of criminal justice.
May 17, 1967	COMMONS
We have adopted the English system of criminal justice, which is an adversary system; it assumes that the best means of arriving at the truth of the case is by contest between the prosecution and the accused in open trial. In fact, of course, many of these contests are notoriously unequal. But I may say that at least one of the long standing bases of inequality has been met in part in my own province at least by the new legal aid system. I am not referring specifically to that problem, but rather to the importance of ensuring that the accused, rich or poor, be not held in custody without the opportunity to secure the assistance of independent legal advice.
Curiously, we set great store by the common law canon that no man shall be compelled to testify against himself, and then ignore the fact that the fairness of the trial, in this adversary contest, may be irretrievably prejudiced before trial by the gap in the law which permits the police to hold the accused incommunicado and subject to a variety of pressures, not excluding the physical, designed to break down his will to resist the state.
My suggestion is that the criminal law should impose a positive obligation upon the police to advise an arrested person of his legal right to have counsel and to facilitate his early contact with counsel. I do not accept the adequacy of the traditional one telephone call referred to in the O'Connor case. It may indeed be a lot easier to secure convictions under the present system, but I would remind hon. members that the function of our criminal process is not to secure convictions but rather to do justice.
A word should be spoken here about organized crime. The hardened criminal is far less subject to the psychological pressure of arrest than is the person who is in conflict with the law for the first time. The professional knows he does not have to talk and that any inducements offered to him by the police are illusory. He may well have greater cause to fear physical violence, but then he may be more hardened to it. Not without reason, he may have cause to believe that his associates already have set in motion the process of habeas corpus or otherwise to secure his freedom. Once again, the very class against whom law enforcement officers cite the law as being required is frequently least subject to it.
It seems to me these are two aspects in which the power given the state unreasonably outweighs the rights of the individual. I have 27053-2U

The second of the major areas in which I feel that our slowness in law reform has worked prejudice for the individual has been that of the civil law under federal jurisdiction. Here again I should like to pick two examples: The priority over other creditors which the crown claims for taxes; and, the heavy stick which crown expropriators swing against small property owners. In respect of the first, a brief review of the federal taxing statutes illustrates what an advantage the treasury claims over other creditors. With regard to income tax and sales tax, for example, the respective laws provide that all taxes, penalties and costs can be claimed by the crown as a debt due in either the exchequer court or other competent court.
In the case of income tax, what the Department of National Revenue commonly does is to issue a certificate that the tax has not been paid. That certificate simply is registered in the court as proof that there is a sum due. It is entirely equivalent to the situation of a businessman who has sued and obtained a judgment for a debt. The difference is that the crown is given the right to skip the ordinary court proceedings and has the amount of the debt set at what it claims, not at what a court has found. This situation works a particular hardship on other businesses in the case of the bankruptcy of a debtor business. Under the Bankruptcy Act the crown is given a priority over other creditors, so, with only a limited body of assets left, the crown can move in and claim payment in full before any of the suppliers of the bankrupt business can collect a nickel. This kind of bad debt which a business failure generates falls particularly heavily on the small supplier who has neither the leverage to compel earlier repayment nor the financial resources to sustain a loss. The inherent weakness of his position becomes a disaster when the agents of the government move in like a flock of gulls and eat up all the assets.
In another situation, the priority given for government taxes works a particular hardship in the case of the intrepid creditor pursuing the hidden assets of a chronic non-payer. The writ of extent, which is the authority issued by the exchequer court to collect the tax debt against property, can be used by the department to claim prior security in hidden assets smoked out by an energetic creditor. The creditor does all the work and the revenuers move in to reap the benefit, like a
May 17. 1967

The Address-Mr. D. S. Macdonald bunch of in-laws. But I hasten to say, quite unlike my in-laws.
As between the small businessman and the government, why should the government have all those advantages? Why should not the government be confined to the same rights as any other creditor? I suggest that the respective taxing statutes should be changed to take away the crown's priority for taxes and put it in the same position as other creditors. Surely the important principle here in connection with bankruptcy or non-payment of debts is who can best afford to bear the loss, the small businessman or the vast resources of the government? The answer is obvious.
It seems to me that the wide array of pre-emptive weapons which the tax collectors have been given has grown up not as a result of conscious policy, but through the draftsman's habit of sticking into the various taxing acts rights which were in the original precedent. I think the time has come to reverse that process.
Another example of unfair advantage between government and a citizen is in the case of expropriating small holdings. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Woolliams) already has set out a critique of the expropriation procedures and has questioned some of the basic principles. I do not intend to cover the ground again. What I should like to refer to is the unfair position in which a person of limited means finds himself when faced with the land taking juggernaut.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
As the hon. member for Bow River has stated, it is the policy of federal expropriation authorities to make a first offer which, on any objective standard, is absurdly below the real value of the property. In the case of larger holdings in the hands of people with financial resources, their bargaining position is better because they have recourse to legal proceedings in the exchequer court, and in the general perspective of reported expropriation cases the landholders seem to have done pretty well.
But in the cases of smaller properties of $3,000 or $5,000 value, the exchequer court is not an option because the very cost of the proceedings would eat up the award. I have a suspicion, for example, that the National Capital Commission in its expropriation for the Ottawa river driveway was in a position to force small cottage holders into settlements that on an objective basis would not be regarded as fair. The problem in this type of

case is that there is no objective basis such as a court hearing in which the fairness of an offer can be tested. What is called for, it seems to me, is some sort of small claims tribunal for expropriations so that by an inexpensive and relatively rapid procedure values could be ascertained if no settlement is reached. Perhaps the Tax Appeal Board could serve as an example of the type of relatively informal tribunal in which these claims could be adjudicated.
In each of the instances which I have given the existing procedures are unduly rigid. The state has, it seems to me, armed itself with far heavier weapons than effective government requires, and the use of the weapons does needless damage.
The final aspect of my remarks, Mr. Speaker, would be with regard to an administrative review procedure, which was referred to in the speech from the throne of April, 1965, but I regret was not mentioned in the last speech from the throne. Certainly the critical nature of the problem has not diminished. We have heard discussions from time to time of a possible administrative procedure for Canada and three foreign examples have been cited, namely the Scandinavian institution of ombudsman, the American federal example of administrative review procedure, and the French system of the conseil d'etat.
Looked at objectively I would say that the third is probably the best precedent and certainly the most successful, but perhaps we should in this regard invoke the caution that the institutions of other states should not be copied without a very profound appreciation of their historical evolution and of the society in which they were produced.
First with regard to the ombudsman, this has certainly been very much in vogue, but how much do some of its advocates really know about it? I would suggest that in view of the nature of the problems in Canada there are reasons why the ombudsman would not be desirable. In Canada the ombudsman must be bilingual, he must be able to deal with a broader range of problems, larger geography and larger population than in the case of some of those countries which already have an ombudsman. Countries like Denmark and New Zealand are homogeneous, unilingual, unitary states of relatively small size and geography. In countries such as these the system appears to work well, but in the case of a country the size of Canada the problem is one of sheer volume, which will therefore require
May 17, 1967

more than one person; it will require, in essence, a panel. To this extent it begins to resemble the conseil d'etat. There is the further problem that if you have more than one person acting in this role there is the difficulty of assuring uniformity of treatment and continued efficiency of the system.
The American administrative procedure act that has been put forward can, I think, be dismissed fairly rapidly because of its limited application. In essence it provides an entry into the general legal system, but these administrative proceedings in the United States have been notable for their complexity, length of time and amount of legal costs. The history of the conseil d'etat has, in my opinion, been distinguished by a very high quality of performance, rapidity of dispatch and relatively low expense. The essentials in this type of administrative review are speed and low cost. This, if I may say so as a member of the profession, should at once rule the lawyers out. In this regard I would say that the Tax Appeal Board, for example, has not been a success when judged by this standard because it is too much like a court.
There must be consistency of judgment. This is why I make the choice of a conseil d'etat over an ombudsman. If you want to assure equal treatment for all cases across the country, in my opinion the conseil d'etat is the best system because cases are dealt with by a panel. There must be equality of treatment in this respect and there should be ease of access to the tribunal.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, the cost of appearing before the tribunal should not only be inexpensive but I would suggest there should be a system instituted which would not prevent a person of limited means taking advantage of the system. I would suggest that in this regard there should be something perhaps in the nature of veterans advocates who are now available to deal with applications to the Canadian Pension Commission. This type of institution might be extended for the purpose of general administrative reviews.
The practical and essential characteristic of a good administrative review procedure is surely obtained through the production of documents. Surely in any case affecting the individual and the state there should be the production of documents. The individual should have the right to have produced to him the government's file about himself. In the long run the mere right to the production of documents is perhaps the individual's best opportunity for an administrative review. The
The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner exceptions, of course, will be in security cases and a limited number of other cases where the security of the state must be pre-eminent, such as cases concerning defence and negotiations between states and others in the field of external affairs, and private and personal information relating to other individuals. I am not satisfied that at the present time there is an effective means for protecting the individual in matters of Canadian administration.
These, Mr. Speaker, are some of the points I should like the government to examine for the purpose of introducing legislation that will make the right of the individual pre-eminent over the great power of the state.

Mr. Speaker, I would adhere to the argument I made earlier. I think the more efficacious institution has been that of the conseil d'etat. I would like to see an administrative tribunal made up of more than one individual; I would like to see it made up of a panel of individuals who could share the same, I hesitate to use the word "jurisprudence" but who would have the same philosophic approach to administration. In this way I think there would be consistency applied to cases across the country. The ombudsman system has received a great deal of popular support, but I am sure the conseil d'etat could be made to work more effectively in a country of our size and population.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in the debate on the speech from the throne I intend to deal to a great extent with the subjects of agriculture and transportation. In opening my remarks I
May 17, 1967

The Address

Mr. J. H. Horner
would say that I agree with the previous speaker and have grave doubts that the ombudsman system would be a solution to all constitutional problems and problems of constituents, in view of the continuous build-up of bureaucracy by this government, provincial and municipal governments.
Having said that, I shall leave that subject and concern myself with the question of agriculture. We notice in the speech from the throne that some mention is made of agriculture. I am pleased to hear the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) is going to set up a fact finding policy group which will be able to devise an agricultural policy for him, something which he has been unable to do in the 21 months he has been in office. If one were to study his background he would find that the minister was born and raised in Toronto and that he is a lawyer by profession. Later he moved to the small town of Arnprior. So one can readily see that he has had very little to do with agriculture, and therefore is at a loss to devise an agricultural policy for Canada. I as a western farmer have often wished that the former minister of agriculture had the silver tongue of the present minister. Perhaps the combination of the former minister's knowledge and the present minister's silver tongue might have produced a spokesman for the farmers of Canada. We in western Canada have recognized the grass roots knowledge of the agricultural industry possessed by the former minister of agriculture, who is now a senator. Unfortunately he was not able to provide us with leadership, partly owing to the fact that he was unfamiliar with parliamentary procedure and thus was unable to transmit his ideas to paper.
The present minister is given to the use of verbiage and very little else. So I take heart, with many other western farmers, in that part of the speech from the throne in which it is said that the Minister of Agriculture will be charged with the project of setting up a special task force which will be recommending policies to meet agricultural goals. I hope that after 21 months in office the minister will have found himself and placed his feet firmly on the ground. I sincerely hope he will be able to deal with the agricultural problems which are facing this nation.
There are grave and serious problems before us. Never before have we had a society so affluent and so able as the one in which we live today. Yet, never before have we seen so much unrest in the agricultural industry.

Milk prices have been low and subsidies have been paid. Nevertheless the farmers are prepared to march on Ottawa. We must try to analyse the problems which confront our farmers. Wheat marketings have been higher than was expected a few years ago; yet there is dissatisfaction among the wheat farmers. The recent international wheat agreement recommended an increase of 21 or 22 cents in the price of wheat. When the president of the Alberta wheat pool was informed of this by a newspaperman he said he could not believe it, that he did not think Canada would accept so small an increase. I point this out, Mr. Speaker, to convince you and the rest of the house that wheat farmers are not satisfied, nor are dairy farmers. I could go down the list and mention the vegetable growers, the beef producers and others who are dissatisfied. We find ourselves in an affluent society, at a time when our economy is booming, and yet every segment of the agricultural industry is dissatisfied. The minister is unable to devise a policy, and so our hopes lie in the speech from the throne in which we are told that a special task force will be set up to try to devise a policy. It is the first time in Canada that we have found it necessary to import butter, eggs and all kinds of vegetable crops. The prices of the staple commodities which can still be exported are going down, and there is dissatisfaction all across the board.
In recommending an increased price for wheat the international wheat agreement did not specifically state that the committed countries have to buy grain at that price. This is the crux of the problem. Why post the minimum price of over $2 a bushel if the committed countries do not have to purchase grain from the exporting nations at that price? It is nothing more than a guide, and it is a well known fact that in the long run farmers expect to receive half or less than half of the 21 or 22 cents which was negotiated not so long ago.
Recently we have heard rumours that wheat farmers all across Canada will be seeding more wheat this year than ever before. This is very doubtful, in view of the adverse weather conditions which we have suffered in western Canada this year. Nevertheless I am still hopeful that encouragement and leadership will be given by the government, and that farmers will make an all-out effort to seed more wheat because there continues to be a large market for wheat in the world today. We are not told about the goals which
May 17. 1967	COMMONS
the special task force mentioned in the speech from the throne proposes to set for itself. The government is a little late in setting up this task force, to say the least.
Last fall the house dealt with a major transportation bill, and yet there was no mention of it in the speech from the throne. That measure has not been enacted in full. Only part V was enacted; but part I, which sets up the new Canadian Transport Commission and which contains clause 16 giving guarantees to the shipper, has not yet been enacted. Why is the government so reluctant to set up the commission and to get it going? Last fall we were told that this legislation had to be passed by January 1, 1967. I am sure every member of the house realized at that time that the debate was urgent and the bill had to be passed. It was passed on January 31 of this year but it has not been fully implemented by the government. What is the reason for this? Why has there been no enactment of the safeguards, which under clause 16 the bill purported to include for the shippers? Shippers all across Canada are being faced with freight increases. Nevertheless protection is not being accorded them. The new Canadian Transport Commission has not yet been fully appointed, and although the legislation enables the two railways to be competitive they are continuing to set equal freight rates. When I consulted the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission and asked them whether or not this is in accordance with their position, I was informed that they were not sure, that they would like to look into it. If competition is to exist between the two railways-and transportation means a great deal to the agricultural industry-then the Director of Investigation and Research, under the authority of the Combines Investigation Act, should look into the pricing of freight rates by the two major railroads.
Both last year and this year there has been a great deal of concern about food prices. The cost of living index went up considerably last month. What does the speech from the throne say on this subject? It sets out clearly that we are going to have a department of corporate and consumer affairs, stating:
Within this department there will be created an organization responsible for developing new policies and co-ordinating programs undertaken within the federal government to assist the consumer and protect the small investor.

What are we going to do? We are going to put the consumer in a position of being more rigidly opposed to the producer. Everywhere

The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner we go in today's society we find the producer on the short end of the stick. The corporate entity which is going to be set up by this government will mean the placing of one more government body against the primary producer. We will then have the government providing no leadership at all in the field of agriculture. Already we have the government providing weak leadership in the field of wheat production. We have the government providing no leadership at all in the field of transportation. They introduced a piece of legislation to cover the transportation industry in this country, yet they failed to provide safeguards for the shipper. The government has not fully organized the departments to police the transportation companies, yet they were in such a rush to pass this legislation.
So we find agriculture gravely concerned about its future. We find the farmers marching on Ottawa because of milk prices. All across the country the farmers are concerned about the prices they are receiving for their agricultural products in the marketplace. Basically we find the farmers asking for greater bargaining power in the marketplace. This is what they really want-more bargaining power in the marketplace. What is this government going to do about this situation? It would seem, according to the speech from the throne, they are going to do very little, other than establish this task force.
We are told in the speech from the throne that more money will be made available for long term loans under the Farm Credit Act. There is one sentence in the speech that gives one some little hope, and it is this one:
During the present session you will be asked to approve legislation to provide long term loans to agricultural and fisheries associations-
What does that really mean? Are we going to allow the agricultural institutions or organizations to borrow huge amounts of money-and it will take huge amounts of money-to market their own products? If this is what this sentence means, then perhaps there is a ray of hope for the agricultural industry in the speech from the throne. Speaking generally, it is interesting to note how the subject of agriculture is dealt with in various speeches from the throne. One finds that it is dealt with in general terms; there is never anything specific for which the government can be held accountable in the following years.
Last year we saw consumer prices become a real problem. Meat prices were one of the things that consumers thought were too high.
May 17. 1967

The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner I should like to put on the record the amount a family spent on food in 1949. In that year a family spent 24 per cent of its disposable income on food, and in 1965, 20.3 per cent of disposable income was spent on food. Of the amount spent on food in 1949, 22.4 per cent was spent for meat, while in 1965 the amount of the food budget spent on meat was 21.7 per cent. In other words, the percentage of the working man's income spent on food has decreased over the years; also the amount spent on meat has decreased over the years.
These figures would lead one to believe that the consumer is either buying less meat or poorer quality meat. However, this is not the case. In 1946, for example, the average consumption of meat in Canada was 60 pounds per person. In 1960 it was over 80 pounds per person. The consumer was therefore buying more meat with less money than he did back in 1949.
Then, you might ask yourself if the consumer is buying better quality meat. The answer to that is obviously yes. In 1949 about 6.4 per cent of the slaughtered cattle in Canada graded choice, the top grade. In 1965, 33 per cent of the cattle slaughtered graded choice. The farmer's product has increased tremendously in quality, while the consumer has increased the amount he uses. At the same time, the amount he spends on food in relation to the amount he is earning has decreased. Surely one would argue, therefore, that the farmer should have more bargaining power in the marketplace. One would have thought that would be obvious; but this is not the case. He finds he has less and less bargaining power in the marketplace and his product is selling for less and less.
We find monopolies developing in the transportation industry, monopolies developing in the cattle marketing industry, monopolies developing in the milk marketing industry. One has only to study the companies that bottle and pasteurize the milk the dairy farmers haul in, to realize the truth of this statement. We find that the monopolies developing are encouraged by this government. For example, in the meat industry one could cite Canada Packers and one could go into the set-up of Safeway stores and their purchases of many of the dairies throughout Canada. The transportation industry speaks for itself. No action has been taken by this government to watch over the competitive factors that must be the key to that industry.
Returning to the beef packing industry, last year Canada Packers told the consumer prices


committee that they handle 28 per cent of the slaughtering of beef animals in Canada. They are prepared to maintain their control of that 28 per cent. In the United States one observes the packing plants moving into the feed lot business. Last year a Senate committee studied the whole problem of whether or not packing plants in the United States should be permitted into the beef feeding industry. Today in Canada we see the packing plants moving more and more into this feeding business.
The farm paper called Country Guide, which is published in Winnipeg, produced an article which clearly set out the fact that Canada Packers had attempted to control meat prices. They realized they could control meat prices if they had a source of supply to keep their packing plants busy. Today in Canada we see the packing plants purchasing more cattle and operating more feed lots than ever before. They have a fully integrated business. Perhaps this procedure is economically justifiable if one is the operator of a packing plant, but it puts the primary producer at a grave disadvantage. This is one more instance in which we find the primary producer on the short end of the stick. It is no wonder the farmers are demanding more bargaining power in the marketplace. We see the farmers in the United States and Canada coming out with a resolution that they will not buy farm machinery. They feel this is the only weapon they can exercise to try to convince the authorities.
Really, though, this is a negative approach. If they need new machinery to take the place of hired help or reduce the number of man hours needed to produce their commodities, then the most efficient thing for them to do is to buy new equipment. If one really wanted to analyse the situation, then ceasing to buy new machinery to reduce the cost of production is really a negative approach. It may be successful however, in convincing the authorities, in a sense, that this is a serious factor in the economy of this country.

The agricultural industry still employs more people in Canada than any other industry. Yet the government is paying less and less attention to this basic industry, the industry on which Canada was founded and which still has a major part to play in society. It is often said by the experts, by professors and by anyone who feels he can offer advice to another industry, that the agricultural industry must become more efficient and must
May 17. 1967	COMMONS
modernize. Above all, it is said that there are too many farmers, that the small farms must disappear.
This, Mr. Speaker, is not necessarily so. The farmer is the most efficient producer in society today. It might interest the house to know that I have before me some figures produced by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics relating to the agricultural efficiency index, using the year 1949 as 100. To the question as to whether the efficiency of agriculture increased or decreased compared with other industries, I would answer that the agricultural efficiency index now stands at 276, compared with the general manufacturing index which stands at 176, and the commercial, non-agricultural industry index standing at 152.5. So that since 1949 the agricultural industry has increased in efficiency far more than any other single industry in Canada.
The agricultural industry has also in many cases increased both the quantity and the quality of its products. Yet these experts and professors are telling the farmers that some of the small farms will have to go. The only reason to justify such a suggestion, Mr. Speaker, is if the industry is not increasing in efficiency and is lagging behind society. But this is not the case; the industry has increased its efficiency tremendously.
What the industry does lack, however, is power at the market place.
The agricultural industry was shortchanged by this new wheat agreement which provides a 22 cents a bushel increase, announced with great fanfare last week. The president of one of the biggest marketing agencies in Alberta exclaimed that surely this was not so, that Canada would not agree to the stated amount. He said that they know we need more. Yet Canada did agree, Mr. Speaker, and naturally the wheat farmers are disappointed, as they should be.
Last session this house enacted a transportation bill to aid the railways, but the primary producer was once again on the short end of the stick. We see the milk marketing situation going from bad to worse, with no real intervention being made by the government to police the operation, and monopolies are moving into this industry to a greater and greater extent.
The Minister of Agriculture announced in Winnipeg that there will be no further subsidies to the milk producers. Naturally, Mr. Speaker, that made them happy-happy in their efforts to rid Canada of the present

The Address-Mr. J. H. Horner government. That is really about all that could make them happy. What they need is more power at the marketplace. If they cannot market their milk and milk products under more suitable arrangements than at present, Mr. Speaker, then they should be given a subsidy. If they are to be asked to subsidize the consumers of Canada, then they in turn should be subsidized. They should not be required to produce the primary products of this country at a rate which will not give them an equitable return for their labours.
We also see agitation from time to time in the cattle marketing industry suggesting that what is required are marketing boards. Let us be quite frank, Mr. Speaker; marketing boards would not raise the price of cattle one little bit in Canada because the price of cattle in Canada bears a close relationship to the price of cattle in the United States.
Today, 10 per cent of the fat cattle sold in Toronto sets the market price for the other 90 per cent. The packing plants are buying cattle direct, either from the feed lots or the farmers. Ten per cent of the fat cattle that are sold set the price for the other 90 per cent that are sold to the packing plants. Calgary calls itself the cattle marketing king of Canada, the centre where more cattle are raised and marketed than anywhere else in Canada. But even in this free enterprise society the packing plants buy 66 per cent of the fat cattle direct from the feed lots or the farmers, and the other 33 per cent set the price. This cannot continue. I would say to this fact finding group, that is going to devise an agricultural policy for a minister who cannot devise one for himself, that we in Canada need a cattle marketing commission to aid the farmers and to give them more power in the marketplace.
A number of years ago we set up wheat pools for the marketing of wheat in western Canada. That was followed by the wheat board, which was designed to give more power to the farmers in the marketplace in marketing their wheat. It now appears that it is not the wheat board that negotiates wheat prices, but that in many instances it is the government of Canada that is the sole negotiator of those prices. Two years ago this government failed to argue its case with the United States government and as a result the price slipped something like 17 cents a bushel. This was due to the inactivity on the part of the minister of trade and commerce at that time.

I suggest that agriculture has really become a less important cabinet portfolio than it was. The government are setting up new departments, most of which are a hodgepodge of other departments. The government set up the Department of Industry, which is a hodgepodge of the former Department of Trade and Commerce. The Department of Manpower and Immigration has come into being, and this is a combination of the former departments of labour and immigration. We now see another department is to be created -for a department, in essence, is what it is-a consumer affairs department. We have also set up a Department of Forestry and Rural Development.
I am afraid, Mr. Speaker, that in the building up of all these departments less and less importance is being attached to the Department of Agriculture. I would urge this task force to give speedy aid to the Minister of Agriculture.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks, I must, like all my colleagues, congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I do so with great pleasure, inasmuch as everyone is unanimous that the hon. members for Bu-rin-Burgeo and Nicolet-Yamaska (Messrs. Jamieson and Cote) have fulfilled their task exceptionally well and have brought honour to the people of their respective constituencies.
Mr. Speaker, this session of the centennial of confederation, to my mind, is a very special one. It should, I think, be one of the outstanding events of 1967 and help enhance parliament in the eyes of the Canadian people, not so much by the quantity of legislation which will be enacted as by the atmosphere it will achieve across Canada namely an atmosphere of understanding, dialogue and confidence in our institutions and in public men, and finally a guarantee of a better future in the economic and social fields.
Perusal of the speech from the throne shows a noticeable intention of the government to create such an atmosphere. Realism

was sought by the avoidance of over-simplification of the problems and a general review indicated the considerable task remaining to be done, if the lives of all Canadians are to be improved as they should be.
Obviously, some people have claimed as usual that the speech from the throne offered nothing extraordinary or exceptional. But, on the whole, the comments are favourable on the government's listing of its responsibilities in different areas and of its determination in finding final solutions.
Towards the end of the speech from the throne he was reading, His Excellency the Governor General, to whom I would pay homage for his appointment and for the way in which he fulfils his duties, quoted the remarks of the first Governor General of Canada. It is surprising to realize to what extent this 100 year old text is still applicable today, in this centennial year. That is why, Mr. Speaker, I take the liberty of quoting them again:
Within our borders peace, security and prosperity prevail, and I fervently pray that your aspirations may be directed to such high and patriotic objects, and that you may be endowed with such a spirit of moderation and wisdom as will cause you to render the great work of union-
Those words were spoken 100 years ago.
-which has been achieved, a blessing to yourselves and your posterity, and a fresh starting point in the moral, political and material advancement of the people of Canada.
As you can see, the centennial message refers to peace, security, prosperity, aspiration, moderation, wisdom and finally a fresh start.
That fresh start is just as real today as it was 100 years ago, but today we also have to face an overall change in our twentieth century world where everything is put to test and where only progressive and determined men will manage to get the confidence of the people.
The time of small electoral promises and great oratory is gone, because many of our problems have a world or North American background and the people expect us to face them in a serious and responsible manner. When looking back, we can easily appreciate and assess the progress made in the last 100 years. Our country has reached a standard of living which is coveted by other countries in the world. We are still developing rapidly and there is more in store for us in the future.
Such assertion is surely an actual fact which deserves a celebration in this centennial year, but we must not stop there,
May 17, 19G7

because the challenge of the years to come, especially in the economic field, goes far beyond what we can imagine today.
There is also, Mr. Speaker, the problem of our constitutional evolution, which many put in the forefront on account of its effects on the relationship between our various levels of government, and its consequences-which is of significance-on the formulation of future policies in the various fields of jurisdiction.
Yet, it seems easy for some to extol overall solutions, such as writing immediately a new constitution. But I wonder how we could achieve this in a short time, when we have yet to agree on a formula to amend the present constitution, precisely because the province of Quebec fears that it would lose, through future amendments, some of the rights it now holds.
In addition, so far as I know, promoters of a new constitution have not yet put forward definite proposals that might serve as a basis for an immediately study.
As far as I am concerned, I believe it is our duty, as members of this house, to work within the bounds of the present constitution and to continue, under the skilful leadership of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), to make the country progress economically and socially, while doing our utmost to maintain a spirit of co-operation, of dialogue with the provinces.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that this centennial session is the appropriate occasion to pay tribute to all the great Canadians, to all those who contributed to our country's development during the last hundred years and particularly to those who assumed successively the functions of prime minister of Canada.
We have here in this house the present Prime Minister and his predecessor, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), two Canadians who spent their whole life serving the nation, and I think it is our duty to thank them for it and to pay tribute to them.
To come back to the debate on the government policy stated in the speech from the throne, I find it impossible to deal with the 25 or so matters mentioned therein. That is why I will limit my remarks to some specific points.
First of all, I was very happy to see emphasized the need for a revision of the rules of the house, and I hope we may agree on certain changes which will make our proceedings more efficient.

The Address[DOT]-Mr. Laniel
The preface to the second edition of a book distributed by the Interparliamentary Union entitled "Parliament", which is a comparative study of the structure and mode of operation of representative institutions in 55 countries, says that:
Parliamentary reform, greater control by parliament over the executive, new parliamentary procedures to meet greater needs-all these are being studied and greatly discussed.
A little further on, there is this passage:
The institution which best represents a nation and serves its true interests is not necessarily one which has been laboriously developed during a determined period in history. On the contrary, it is one which has changed and developed through constant effort in the light of experience accumulated under changing conditions.
This means that the problem of parliamentary reform is universal and that we should examine this question in the best interest of our democratic system. Personally, I think that, in addition to the changes which should be made in the rules of the House of Commons concerning the elimination and restriction of certain traditional debates which lead nowhere, the elimination of certain stages in the passing of government legislation, and the consideration and adoption of estimates, it is of the utmost importance that we re-examine thoroughly the status of the standing committees of the House of Commons. Those committees provide us with an instrument which can be very useful to parliament, and I think that the house should modify their structure so as to grant them a greater degree of autonomy, greater freedom in organizing their work and the funds necessary to hire research personnel.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
As chairman of the committee on veterans affairs this past session, I would have liked the committee to sit from last fall until the end of the session, a few days ago, in order to complete the comparative study of our veterans pension plan.
During our trip to Europe in July 1966, we gathered in various countries some very interesting information on the benefits enjoyed there by veterans. It would have been most useful for the committee to have had the opportunity, on returning to Canada, to study this matter more thoroughly and to ask the departmental officials to testify before it, so as to obtain more information and their views.
Since we had already referred the departmental estimates back to the house and submitted our report on Dr. Richardson's study on Hong Kong veterans, we had no authority
May 17, 1967

The Address

Mr. Laniel
to meet, and we lost four or five months during which we could have prepared more properly for the work still to be done on the Woods report to be submitted shortly.
Mr. Speaker, in that connection, I must say I was disappointed at not finding in the speech from the throne any reference to veterans, to those who went overseas to defend their country and democracy and who sacrificed part of their health to enable younger generations to live in peace and freedom. I fully agree that the government is concerned with economic development, manpower, scientific progress, trade, etc., but I feel that nowadays those who served their country as gloriously as our Canadian soldiers are easily forgotten.
It is true that we pay them a very moving tribute on Remembrance Day, but after all, those of our veterans who suffered the hardships of war and came back marked for life should not be considered as second class citizens. At times, I deplore this modem world in which everything seems to be discarded in favour of technology and electronic machines and everything is judged and appraised according to its effectiveness, output and future potential.
It is true, Mr. Speaker, that our assistance program for veterans is better than in certain countries, if not in most. May I add that these benefits must relate to the North American context and bring about a measure of wellbeing equivalent to the average of the population.
People talk about retraining and increase of workers' income, but the fact remains that the veteran is the worse paid Canadian considering the services he rendered to the nation, to society and to the world. Retrained or not, he will never regain what war atrocities took away from him.
I recognize that the Woods commission was created to consider the functioning and administration of the Canadian Pension Commission, and that we could hardly expect in the speech from the throne proposals for important reform to existing legislation.
At this stage, I take the opportunity to inform all members and perhaps to correct certain remarks made yesterday, that the Woods commission enjoys the full confidence of the veterans' associations and especially the Canadian Legion. I know that these same associations readily accept that this report may be somewhat delayed, because they are convinced that the commission has carried out its work in an unbiased and responsible

way, and that the recommendations will be more effective for it.
However, Mr. Speaker, I think that, in this centennial year, the speech from the throne should have included at least a statement of intent, and even certain projects concerning matters not provided for in the studies of the Woods commission.
Before passing to another matter, I shall simply mention a few, namely: the basic rate of pensions and allowances, which should have been changed long ago, a system allowing for automatic pension increases based on a definite standard, such as the cost of living, salaries, etc., and let us not forget the project of a memorial for the veterans of the two world wars in the national capital, and the eventual development of the Vimy park, that Canadian soil to the memory of veterans in France.
Therefore, I hope that before the end of the year the government will bring forward some concrete measures to show its concern for war veterans, through the good offices of the minister in charge of this department.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne refers to regional development, foreign investments, retraining of workers, for which the government should be congratulated, but I take the liberty of adding that, at the same time, we should not forget our responsibilities, especially as concerns existing industries, and our duty to maintain in our country an environment conducive to their development.
I refer especially to the textile industry which is now experiencing a very heavy competition from foreign imports, especially Japanese, which have increased by 72.7 per cent from 1964 to 1966 inclusive. It is a known fact that the industry which was going through a serious stagnation period in 1950 has succeeded in recovering and investing from 1961 to 1966 an amount of $635 million. However, the present situation shows that a major deterioration can be expected in 1967, unless the government takes some action to protect that industry which provides employment for 200,000 persons.
I know that the government is conscious of the problem and that it will succeed in taking a firm stand during negotiations which are under way with Japan, so as to avoid disastrous effects for the Canadian textile industry.
In the field of urban development, I am pleased to congratulate the government for the step taken last year, when it signed an
May 17, 1967	COMMONS
agreement with the government of the province of Quebec among others, in order to undertake pilot surveys in certain municipalities which will lead us, I hope, to the establishment of a general program of urban development throughout the province. In the past, such an endeavour had generally been left to private enterprise or to individuals but it is advisable that the two levels of government should take some practical measures in that field which are bound to complete the services already offered under the National Housing Act through the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
As the problem of water pollution, which seems to be on the priority list of the government, cannot be solved at the national level only, I hope that the central government, in addition to passing this new water legislation, as announced in the speech from the throne, and in addition to co-operating with the provinces, will not forget to amend the National Housing Act, which provides for municipal loans for building water purification plants and sewage systems. As many initiatives in this field can originate at the municipal level,
I am of the opinion that the remission of part of the capital and interest during the construction period, which is now 25 per cent, should be raised to at least 50 per cent or more, for I am convinced that will mean concrete services and give immediate results.

With regard to agriculture, Mr. Speaker, at a time when Ontario and Quebec farmers talk of marching on the Canadian capital because of the dairy policy of the government, it is still comforting to see that a special team, headed by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene) will be entrusted with defining our objectives in the field of agriculture and with recommending such programs as will be considered necessary to attain those goals. Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people are certainly not indifferent about what is going on in Canadian politics and in each capital throughout the country, as people everywhere, they expect from those various levels of government measures which will help them continue their efforts towards the progress and development of the country. I think, however, that they are worried about a problem which affects them perhaps more deeply than is imagined, namely that of the political context in which we have been living for the last few years, where overbidding, shattering statements and public conflicts make the headlines every day and give a false idea of our Canadian society.
It is true that we are now going through a period of political evolution, that many matters are being re-examined and that the aspirations of the various Canadian groups are becoming increasingly distinct. But I wonder nevertheless whether we might not succeed in solving our problems in a more discreet and perhaps more enlightened manner around a negotiation table, through open and constructive discussion.
Of course, it is sometimes necessary in political circles to arouse public opinion. But I wonder if it is really enlightened by some of our attitudes and our off-hand approach to certain problems, especially constitutional problems.
At this point, I am not speaking of those who do not believe in Canada and who would destroy it; I am thinking mostly of our public men who are in power and who all seem to want the same thing, namely to reinforce Canadian unity through a better understanding of each others' problems.
In this year of the centennial of confederation, during Expo '67 whose theme is "Man and his World", at a time when His Holiness Pope Paul VI is appealing for brotherhood throughout the world, should we not open up our minds to the world by starting to practice those great principles of brotherhood which were suggested, particularly by the Canadian bishops in their letter to all Canadians on the occasion of the centennial of confederation?
I shall close by quoting a paragraph of that letter:
It is not being brotherly to be content with abstract formulas, verbal statements or sterile hopes, be they as generous as the whole world is big. It is not being brotherly to love mankind in the abstract or to make noble dreams of solidarity with far-off brothers while taking an attitude of meanness or hostility towards those nearer to us. True brotherhood must create immediate and practical

But, on the other hand, to conform to the Gospel, concrete brotherhood must not be restrictive. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although wishing to join sincerely in the congratulations extended to the mover and seconder of the address in reply, and of course wholeheartedly in the cordial sentiments expressed to His Excellency, nevertheless no one participating in the debate on the throne speech itself can fail to feel and to express regret that the speech should be so bare of outline of any statement of objectives which might give some encouragement and leadership to the Canadian people as we enter upon the one hundredth year of our history.
Indeed one of the things the throne speech has done, and unfortunately about the only thing it has done, is to increase the sense of concern, the sense of frustration of the Canadian people who are looking, longing and waiting so anxiously to see some signs that their government is going to come to grips with the problems that concern the people and give some program to launch us on the direction that the country needs in the second century of our existence.
People are looking and waiting to see these signs, Mr. Speaker, I have been across Canada quite extensively during the past few weeks and I find that the Canadian people are deeply concerned about the attitudes of governments and the role and relationship that should prevail between government and people. They are deeply concerned about the weight of government, the weight of the different levels of government but primarily of the federal government on their backs. They are deeply concerned over the inefficiency of government. They are deeply concerned because they find that notwithstanding increasing expenditures and increasing taxes, the problems that require action by government do not seem to be receiving the attention of the government.

The people are concerned because the problems mount, and the lack of action mounts in direct relationship, it appears, to the cost of government. They are concerned over taxes. They are concerned over the fact that property taxes across Canada this year have gone up an average of 11 per cent in a single year as municipalities, especially with inadequate revenue bases, seek to discharge all the responsibilities saddled upon them and which should no longer be saddled upon them.
The people are concerned over government spending, and over the fact that federal estimates for all expenditure this year have gone up over 13 per cent in a single year, with no encouragement to hope that there will be any increase in efficiency or real action on the problems that concern the people.
They are concerned over the cost of living which mounts steadily, unheeded and unchecked by anything done by government, indeed with the increase stimulated by the kind of programs that this government in Ottawa has been following. The cost of living has gone up over one point in just this past month, probably a record increase in a single month, and the people are concerned because the government appears to be unconcerned about it, unhurried to do anything about it, concerned only to pass the buck. The best contribution the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) could make was to say that the main reason for the increase lay at the door of the increased sales tax put on in the province of Quebec. Mr. Speaker, of course one regrets any increase in sales taxes. But what a feeble and impertinent excuse it is for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), who maintains a 12 per cent sales tax on building materials, construction machinery and equipment, to seek to lay the blame for this sort of thing on a sales tax applied by a province.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
The nonsense of this position is demonstrated by the fact that the increase in the cost of living went up 1.7 points in Montreal. To be sure, perhaps the sales tax in Quebec had something to do with it, but did the sales tax in Quebec account for the fact that the cost of living in Vancouver rose by 1.3 points? Is the minister going to blame that on the province of Quebec, or will he accept his responsibility for the policies which has contributed to the inflationary pressures? When will he accept his responsibility to take action to establish the kind of program and tax policy-a kind of over-all governmental policy-which will give the Canadian people some relief from the
May 17, 1967

crushing burden of government, and which will bring about some efficiency in the spending of the money which is collected from them in the way of taxes?
This is what the Canadian people are concerned about. Later in my remarks I should like to suggest some of the progressive things which should be done to give us a sense of direction and prosperity as we enter upon our centennial year in the second century of our history. First, I believe it is necessary to analyse the things that concern our people, in order to understand what the problems are in the sphere of governmental responsibility in respect of which it is essential that action be taken. I am satisfied that there is a growing feeling on the part of the Canadian people that they want a government with a basic philosophy, a basic understanding, and a declaration of what should be the role of the government and the relationship of that government to the people-a government which will set forth the principles it intends to follow and state its position as to whether it intends to do more and more things for more and more people at more and more cost, or whether in fact it is going to have confidence in the ability of the Canadian people to do things for themselves and be guided by the belief that the primary responsibility of the government is to establish the atmosphere and lay down the general policies under which the Canadian people in fact can do more and more things for themselves.
This is what concerns our people; they want more freedom to move. They feel the crushing weight of government on their backs. You, Mr. Speaker, I, and everybody in this house know that the people of this country have a tremendous talent and ability-a latent talent-for doing things. The Canadian people should be able to move; they should be given the freedom to move. They want to be free to move ahead in order to insure their own future. This is the instinct which is in the heart of every Canadian. He wishes to do this so that he will be better off at the end of the year than he was at the beginning. He wants freedom; he wants the government to get off his back, at least a little, so that he will be relieved of the weight which grinds him down and freezes him in his present position.
Primarily there is one way in which Canadians can be allowed to move and improve their own position; that is, if the government will follow a general policy, a basic philosophy, which leaves to the people a little
The Address-Mr. Fulton more freedom at the end of the year, a little more to invest for themselves, and a little more to enable them to have a stake in and be part of this growing and developing nation, so that they will be able to insure their future. That is what the Canadian people want. The government should set forth and follow that basic policy. It should encourage the movement forward of Canadians and the investment by Canadians in a stake in Canada itself.
But, Mr. Speaker, instead what do we find? We are served up with this throne speech, this mealy mass of words. There is no sense of direction, no clarity of position and no indication of any real understanding of the very basic nature of the country and its people. The throne speech in fact can lay only one claim; that is, if the philosophy of the present government is to be followed, the government which already occupies so many fields which it should not occupy will occupy the few remaining fields in which it does not yet intrude. That is the whole policy in the speech from the throne-a further extension of government intrusion into the management of people's affairs.
Can't you just see the Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet when they sat down to draft the speech from the throne. Perhaps this is the reason the Prime Minister called back the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon). Perhaps he wanted him to write it from the left wing point of view, along with the points of view of the other members of the government. You can just see them sitting there as they ponder it. One can picture the Prime Minister asking the President of the Privy Council what should be their basic theme, and the President of the Privy Council replying that perhaps it should be a further extension of the government's activities. I can just hear the Prime Minister replying, "I guess you are right. All right, we have made a first class mess of the others; let us see what kind of a mess we can make of these." This is precisely what will be done; they have started already. They certainly are making a first class mess of their own cabinet, and of the doctrine of cabinet solidarity and responsible government.
What a mockery it is when a Prime Minister excuses, apologizes, and walks around the fact that one of his senior ministers has come out with a statement on an important fundamental matter of policy which is radically different from the policy enunciated by that responsible spokesman the Secretary of

Let us build on that concept. There can be no doubt that this concept is still valid and viable today. That is what must be preserved and built upon, because it is a splendid and uniquely Canadian concept.
